Let $\bm{T}$ be a non-defective variable type. 
Consider the second moment of judicious configurations under $\mathbb{P}_{\mathscr{D}}$, restricted to the near-independent regime $\bm{I}_0$ (as has been the case throughout this section). Let $\mathbf{P}$ denote the empirical measure of configurations $(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\varsigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})$, taken over all variables $v$ of type $\bm{T}$, that gives the maximal contribution to this restricted second moment. For $e\in\delta v$ let $\bm{\zeta}_e$ denote the marginal law of $(\varsigma_e,\bm{L}_e)$ under $\mathbf{P}$, and suppose it satisfies
	\begin{align}
	
	1-\bm{\zeta}_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\,|\,\bm{L})
	&\le \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^k}\,,\\
	
	\hat{\iota}_{e,\bm{L}}
	\equiv \bm{\zeta}_e\Big(\varsigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\}^2
		\,\Big|\,\bm{L}\Big)
	+ \frac{k^4}{4^k}
	&\le \frac1{2^{k(1+\epsilon)}}
	\end{align}
for all $e\in\delta v$ and all $\bm{L}$. Then it must satisfy the estimate
	\begin{equation}
	\bigg|\frac{\mathbf{P}(\sigma_e=\sigma\,|\,\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})}
		{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma^1)
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma^2)
		}-1\bigg| \le \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}
	\end{equation}
for all $\sigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}^2\setminus\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\}$ and all $\bm{L}$.

\begin{proof} As in the statement of the lemma, let us fix a variable $v$ of type $\bm{T}$ that is non-defective. Write
	\begin{equation}
	\smash{\underline{\smash{X}}}_{\delta v}
	\equiv (X_e)_{e\in\delta v}
	\equiv
	\bigg(\Big(\sigma_e,\varsigma_e\Big)
	\bigg)_{e\in\delta v}\,.\end{equation}
Note that, by the rules of Definition~9.1, the configuration 
$\smash{\underline{\smash{X}}}_{\delta v}$ also implicitly encodes $\smash{\underline{\smash{\Sigma}}}_{\delta v}$. In the augmented model where each edge $e=(av)$ is also labelled with the clause type $\bm{L}_e\equiv\bm{L}_a$, denote
	\begin{equation}
	\mathcal{X}\equiv \mathcal{X}_v
	\equiv (\smash{\underline{\smash{X}}}_{\delta v},
		\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})
	\equiv 
	\bigg(
	(X_e)_{e\in\delta v}, 
	(\bm{L}_e)_{e\in\delta v}\bigg)
	\,.\end{equation}
Recall that $\bm{\zeta}_e$ denotes the marginal law of $(\bm{L}_e,\varsigma_e)$ under $\mathbf{P}$. We can write it as
	\[\bm{\zeta}_e(\bm{L},\varsigma)
	\equiv \mathbf{P}\bigg(\bm{L}_e=\bm{L}, 
		\varsigma_e=\varsigma\bigg)
	= \pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_e)
	\bm{\zeta}_e(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})\,.\]
The measure $\mathbf{P}$ must maximize entropy subject to the marginal constraints
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}
	\begin{alignat}{2}
	
	\mathbf{P}(\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
		&=\pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_e)
		\quad&&\textup{for all $\bm{L}$,}\\
	
	\mathbf{P}( (\sigma_e)^i=\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
		&= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e(\sigma^i)
		\quad&&\textup{for all $\bm{L}$
			and all $\sigma^i\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}$,}\\
	
	\mathbf{P}(\varsigma_e=\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
		&= \bm{\zeta}_e(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
		\quad&&\textup{for all $\bm{L}$
		and all $\varsigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\}^2$,}
	
	\end{alignat}}
for all $e\in\delta v$. By the method of Lagrange multipliers, $\mathbf{P}$ must take the form
	\begin{equation}
	\mathbf{P}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},
	\smash{\underline{\smash{\varsigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})
	\cong
	\psi_v(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{e\in\delta v}\Bigg\{
	\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_e\sim\varsigma_e\}
	\psi_e(\bm{L}_e)
	
	\Bigg(
	\prod_{i=1,2}(\beta_e)^i((\sigma_e)^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg)
	\chi_e(\varsigma_e\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg\}	
	\end{equation}
where $\psi_v(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})$ is as in (7.55) from Definition~7.24, and we write $\sigma\sim\varsigma$ to indicate compatibility: formally, it means for both $i=1,2$ that we have $\sigma^i\sim\varsigma^i$ in the sense that the following holds:
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	\varsigma^i=\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}} \quad &\textup{whenever $\sigma^i=\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}$,}\\
	\varsigma^i\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\}
		\quad &\textup{whenever $\sigma^i=\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}$,}\\
	\varsigma^i\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\}
		\quad &\textup{whenever $\sigma^i\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}$.}
	\end{align*}}
We now turn to the construction of the weights in (9.81). We divide the remainder of the argument into a few parts.\smallskip


\noindent\textbf{\textup{Part~1. Single-copy estimates.}}
Let $\nu\equiv(\dot{\nu},\hat{\nu})$ be the vertex empirical measure that gives the maximal contribution to the first moment (of judicious configurations). The edge marginal of $\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$ is the canonical marginal $\omega_{\bm{L},j}={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{\bm{L}(j)}$. Given the mapping from $\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta a}$ to $\smash{\underline{\smash{\varsigma}}}_{\delta a}$ within each clause, the measure $\hat{\nu}_{\bm{L}}$ induces a measure on configurations $\smash{\underline{\smash{\varsigma}}}_{\delta a}$. Let ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_{\bm{L},j}\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_{\bm{L}(j)}$ denote the marginal law of $\varsigma_j$ under this measure; we call this the canonical marginal on $\varsigma^i$ for an edge of type $\bm{t}=\bm{L}(j)$. If $e$ is an edge of type $\bm{t}$ then we also write ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_{\bm{t}}$. Explicitly,
	\begin{align*}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
	&\cong {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
		\Bigg\{
		\prod_{e'\in\delta v\setminus e}
		{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})
		\Bigg\}\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})
	&\cong 
	\dot{q}_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})
	\Bigg\{
	\sum_{e'\in\delta v\setminus e}
		\dot{q}_{e'}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
	\prod_{e''\in\delta v\setminus \{e,e'\}}
	\dot{q}_{e''}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\Bigg\}\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
	&\cong 
	\dot{q}_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
	\Bigg\{
	\sum_{e'\in\delta v\setminus e}
		\dot{q}_{e'}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
		\prod_{e''\in\delta v\setminus \{e,e'\}}
		\dot{q}_{e''}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\Bigg\}\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})
	&\cong {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\})
	\prod_{e'\in\delta v\setminus e}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_{e'}(\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\})
	\Bigg( 1-\frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^k}\Bigg)\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last estimate uses the assumption that $v$ is non-defective, hence nice, so that ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e$ satisfies the estimates of Definition~3.8
for all $e\in\delta v$. It follows that
	\begin{equation}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})
	\end{pmatrix}
	= \begin{pmatrix}
	\Theta(1/2^k)\\
	\Theta(k/2^k)\\
	\Theta(k/2^k)\\
	1 - \Theta(k/2^k)
	\end{pmatrix}\,.\end{equation}
(We also remark that ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})$, although we will not use this fact in what follows.)\smallskip


\noindent\textbf{\textup{Part~2. Single-copy weights.}} We first consider the simpler problem of setting weights in the single-copy model. For this discussion, let $\sigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}$ and $\varsigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\}$, and again write $\sigma\sim\varsigma$ to indicate compatibility.
Given a probability measure ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ over $\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}$, along with a probability measure ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta$ over spins $\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\}$ such that ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})$, we look for weights ${}_\star b$ and ${}_\star x$ such that
	\begin{equation}
	\mu(\sigma,\varsigma)
	\equiv
	\mathbf{1}\{\sigma\sim\varsigma\}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\sigma)
	{}_\star b(\sigma)
	{}_\star x(\varsigma)
	\end{equation}
defines a probability measure over $(\sigma,\varsigma)$ whose marginal on $\sigma$ is ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$, and whose marginal on $\varsigma$ is ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta$. Explicitly, for the $\sigma$-marginal to be ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ we must have the equations
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}) &= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}) {}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}){}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
		= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}) &= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})[{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})
		+{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})]\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}) &={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})[{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
		+{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})]\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}) &={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})[{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
		+{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})]\,.\end{align*}
For the $\varsigma$-marginal to be ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta$ we must have the equations
	\begin{align*}{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})
		&={}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}){}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
		&=[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}) 
			+{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}) ]
			{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})\,,\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})
		&=[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})
		+{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})
	+{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}){}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})
	]{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})\,.
	\end{align*}}
Note also that if we multiply all the ${}_\star b$-weights by a scaling factor and divide all the ${}_\star x$-weights by the same factor, it has no effect on the right-hand side of (9.83), so without loss we can pin down the weights by requiring
${}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})=1$ and ${}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})=1$.
Then, combining the equations for ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})$ gives
	\[
	{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}) =\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})}\,,\quad
	{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}) = \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})}\,.
	\]
Next, comparing the equations for ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})$ gives
	\[
	\frac{{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})}{{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})}
	= \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})/{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})/{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})}
	= \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})}=1\,,
	\]
and we hereafter denote ${}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})\equiv {}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})\equiv{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})$. 
Combining with the equations for 
${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})$, ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})$, and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})$ gives
	\[
	{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})=
	\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})+{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})}
		{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}) + {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})}
	= \frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})}\,,\quad
	{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
	=\frac{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})}{{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})}\,.
	\]
In summary, a valid solution is given by taking
	\begin{align}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})\\
	{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\\
	{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}})={}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}})
	\equiv{}_\star b(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
	\end{pmatrix}
	&= 
	\begin{pmatrix}
	1\\
	[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})]/{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\\
	[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})]/{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})
	\end{pmatrix}
	\stackrel{(9.82)}{=} 
	\begin{pmatrix}
	\Theta(1)\\ \Theta(1) \\ \Theta(1)
	\end{pmatrix}\,,\\
	
	\begin{pmatrix}
	{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})\\
	{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})\\
	{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})\\
	{}_\star x(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}})
	\end{pmatrix}
	&=\begin{pmatrix}
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})/{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})/[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}})]\\
	{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})/[{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})-{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}})]\\
	1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\stackrel{(9.82)}{=} 
	\begin{pmatrix}
	\Theta(1/2^k)\\
	\Theta(k/2^k)\\
	\Theta(k/2^k)\\ 1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\,.\end{align}
Substituting these into (9.83)
gives a measure with the desired marginals ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi$ and ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta$.\smallskip



\noindent\textbf{\textup{Part~3. Initialization in pair model.}} Returning to (9.81), our goal is to construct a sequence of measures
	\[
	\mathbf{P}_t(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},
	\smash{\underline{\smash{\varsigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})
	\cong
	\psi_{v,t}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{e\in\delta v}\Bigg\{
	\psi_{e,t}(\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg(
	\prod_{i=1,2}
	(\beta_{e,t})^i((\sigma_e)^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg)
		\chi_{e,t}(\varsigma_e\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg\}\]
which converges as $t\to\infty$ to the desired solution $\mathbf{P}_\infty\equiv\mathbf{P}$. We will further decompose the $\beta$ weights as
	\[
	(\beta_{e,t})^i( \sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\equiv
	\bigg\{(\dot{\beta}_{e,t})^i( \sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)\bigg\}
	\cdot
	\bigg\{(\hat{\beta}_{e,t})^i( \sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)\bigg\}
	\]
such that $(\hat{\beta}_{e,t})^i$ does not distinguish between $\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}$ and $\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}$, that is, such that
	\[
	(\hat{\beta}_{e,t})^i( \textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	=(\hat{\beta}_{e,t})^i( \textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\equiv(\hat{\beta}_{e,t})^i( \textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\,|\,\bm{L}_e)\,.
	\]
This is clearly an over-parametrization, so the $\dot{\beta}$ and $\hat{\beta}$ weights will not be uniquely determined; we need only find one choice of weights such that the resulting measure (9.81) satisfies the constraints (9.78)--(9.80). The overparametrization will be useful below because it allows for some separation between the analysis of the $\varsigma$-marginals and the analysis of the $(\sigma,\bm{L})$-marginals.

We initialize the construction at $t=0$ as follows.
We first set $\psi_{v,0}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})$ to be equal to $\varphi_v(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})$, which we recall from
(2.18) is simply
the indicator of a valid pair coloring $\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v}$.
For an edge $e$ of type $\bm{t}$, let ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_e\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\pi_{\bm{t}}$ be the canonical marginal on $\sigma^i$, and let ${}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e\equiv{}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_{\bm{t}}$ be the canonical marginal on $\varsigma^i$, as discussed above.
Let ${}_\star b_e$ and ${}_\star x_e$ be the corresponding weights defined by (9.84) and (9.85); in particular, we recall
from (9.84) that ${}_\star b_e$
does not distinguish between $\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}$ and $\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}$. We then set
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{alignat*}{2}
	\psi_{e,0}(\bm{L})
		&\equiv\pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_e)
		\quad
		&&\textup{for all $\bm{L}$,}\\
	(\dot{\beta}_{e,0})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L})
		&\equiv 1
		&&\textup{for
		$i=1,2$,
		all $\bm{L}$,
		and all $\sigma^i\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}$,}\\
	(\hat{\beta}_{e,0})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L})
		&\equiv {}_\star b_e(\sigma^i)\quad
		&&\textup{for
		$i=1,2$,
		all $\bm{L}$,
		and all $\sigma^i\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}$,}\\
	\chi_{e,0}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
		&\equiv 
		{}_\star x_e(\varsigma^1)
		{}_\star x_e(\varsigma^2)\quad
		&&\textup{for all 
		$\bm{L}$ and all $\varsigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\}^2$.}
	\end{alignat*}}
Thus at $t=0$ the measure $\mathbf{P}_0$ will satisfy constraints 
(9.78) and (9.79), but not
(9.80), since we will have
	\[
	\bm{\zeta}_{e,0}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
	\equiv
	\mathbf{P}_0(\varsigma_e=\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
	=\prod_{i=1,2} {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\zeta_e(\varsigma^i)\,,
	\]
which in general is not the same as
$\bm{\zeta}_e(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})$.\smallskip

\noindent\textbf{\textup{Part~4. Update procedure.}}
In this step we will make use of Lemma~9.15, which is stated and proved below. For $t\ge0$ let $\delta_{e,t}$ and $\ddot{\delta}_{e,t}$ denote parameters such that the estimates (9.95)--(9.97) below hold for the error between $\bm{\zeta}_{e,t}(\cdot\,|\,\bm{L})$ versus $\bm{\zeta}_e(\cdot\,|\,\bm{L})$ --- that is to say,
for all clause types $\bm{L}$ that can appear incident to edge $e$, we assume that
	\begin{align}
	
	\max
	\Bigg\{
	\Big|\bm{\zeta}_e(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
		-\bm{\zeta}_{e,t}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})\Big|
	: \varsigma\in\{
	\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}},
	\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize w}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\}
	\Bigg\}
	&\le \frac{k^{O(1)}\delta_{e,t}}{2^k}\,,\\
	
	\max
	\Bigg\{
	\Big|\bm{\zeta}_e(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
		-\bm{\zeta}_{e,t}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})\Big|
	: \varsigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\}^2
	\Bigg\}
	&\le \hat{\iota} \delta_{e,t}\,, \\
	
	\bigg|
		\frac{\bm{\zeta}_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\,|\,\bm{L})}
		{\bm{\zeta}_{e,t}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\,|\,\bm{L})}-1\bigg|
	&\le\ddot{\delta}_{e,t}\,.
	\end{align}
At the initialization $t=0$ 
it follows from (9.73) and (9.74) that
$\delta_{e,t} \le O(1)$
and $\ddot{\delta}_{e,t} \le O(2^{k(1-\epsilon)})$.
Denote
	\begin{equation}
	\bm{\delta}_t
	\equiv\sum_{e\in\delta v}\delta_{e,t}\,,\quad
	\bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t
	\equiv\sum_{e\in\delta v}
		\min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}\,.\quad
	\end{equation}
Let $t\ge0$ be an integer time, and suppose inductively that we have constructed the weights at time $t$. The marginal law on an edge $e\in\delta v$ is given by
	\[
	\mathbf{P}_t(\sigma_e=\sigma,\varsigma_e=\varsigma,\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
	\cong
	\mathbf{1}\{\sigma\sim\varsigma\}
	\dot{q}_{e,t}(\sigma)
	\psi_{e,t}(\bm{L})
	\Bigg(\prod_{i=1,2} (\beta_{e,t})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L})\Bigg)
	\chi_{e,t}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})\,,
	\]
where $\dot{q}_{e,t}$ is the probability measure over $\sigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize c}}\}^2$ defined by 
	\[
	\dot{q}_{e,t}(\sigma)
	\cong
	\sum_{\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v}:
		\sigma_e=\sigma}
	\psi_{v,t}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}})
	\prod_{e'\in\delta v\setminus e}
	\Bigg\{
	\sum_{\bm{L}_{e'}}
	\psi_{e',t}(\bm{L}_{e'})
	\Bigg(\prod_{i=1,2}
	\beta_{e',t}((\sigma_{e'})^i\,|\,\bm{L}_{e'})
	\Bigg)
	\sum_{\varsigma_{e'}:
		\varsigma_{e'} \sim \sigma_{e'}}
	\chi_{e',t}(\varsigma_{e'}\,|\,\bm{L}_{e'})
	\Bigg\}\,.
	\]
The conditional law of $(\sigma_e,\varsigma_e)$ given $\bm{L}_e$ is then given by
	\[
	\mathbf{P}_t(\sigma_e=\sigma,\varsigma_e=\varsigma\,|\,
		\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
	\cong \mathbf{1}\{\sigma\sim\varsigma\}
	\dot{q}_{e,t}(\sigma)
	\Bigg(\prod_{i=1,2}
		(\beta_{e,t})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L})\Bigg)
	\chi_{e,t}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})\,.
	\]
For each $\bm{L}$, we apply Lemma~9.15 (below) to find updated weights $(\hat{\beta}_{e,t+3/4})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L})$ and $\chi_{e,t+3/4}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})$ such that, if we define $(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^i
\equiv (\dot{\beta}_{e,t})^i \cdot (\hat{\beta}_{e,t+3/4})^i$, then 
 the probability measure
	\[
	\tilde{\mu}_{e,t+3/4}
	(\sigma,\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
	\cong
	\mathbf{1}\{\sigma\sim\varsigma\}
	\dot{q}_{e,t}(\sigma)
	\Bigg(\prod_{i=1,2}
	(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L}) 
	\Bigg)
	\chi_{e,t+3/4}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
	\]
has $\varsigma$-marginal exactly $\bm{\zeta}_e(\cdot\,|\,\bm{L})$. The marginal law of $(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})$ at time $t+3/4$ is then given by
	\[
	\mathbf{P}_{t+3/4}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})
	\cong
	\psi_{v,t}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{e\in\delta v}\Bigg\{
	\underbrace{
	\psi_{e,t}(\bm{L}_e)
	\sum_{\varsigma_e:\varsigma_e
		\sim \sigma_e}
	\Bigg(\prod_{i=1,2}
		(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^i((\sigma_e)^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
			\Bigg)
	\chi_{e,t+3/4}(\varsigma_e\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	}_{\cong \hat{q}_{e,t+3/4}(\sigma_e,\bm{L}_e)}
	\Bigg\}\,,
	\]
where $\hat{q}_{e,t}$ is a probability measure over pairs $(\sigma,\bm{L})$. It follows from Lemma~9.15 that
	\begin{equation}
	\widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{q}_{e,t},\hat{q}_{e,t+3/4})
	\le
	\max_{\bm{L}}\left\{
	k^{O(1)}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	\hat{\iota}_{e,\bm{L}}&0\\
	2^k \hat{\iota}_{e,\bm{L}}&0\\
	1&1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	\delta_{e,t}\\
	\ddot{\delta}_{e,t}
	\end{pmatrix}
	\right\}
	\stackrel{(9.74)}{\le}
	k^{O(1)}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	2^{-k(1+\epsilon)}&0\\
	2^{-k\epsilon}&0\\
	1&1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	\delta_{e,t}\\
	\ddot{\delta}_{e,t}
	\end{pmatrix}
	\,.\end{equation}
Then apply Proposition~7.28 (where the $\hat{p}_e$ and $\hat{q}_e$ of 
Proposition~7.28 are given by
$\hat{q}_{e,t}$ and $\hat{q}_{e,t+3/4}$ respectively) to find new weights $\psi_{v,t+1}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}})$, $\psi_{e,t+1}(\bm{L})$, and $(\dot{\beta}_{e,t+1})^i(\sigma^i\,|\,\bm{L})$ such that, if we define
$(\beta_{e,t+1})^i \equiv (\dot{\beta}_{e,t+1})^i(\hat{\beta}_{e,t+3/4})^i$,
then the probability measure
	\[
	\mathbf{P}_{t+1}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\varsigma}}}_{\delta v},\smash{\underline{\smash{\bm{L}}}}_{\delta v})
	\cong
	\psi_{v,t+1}(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v})
	\prod_{e\in\delta v}\Bigg\{
	\psi_{e,t+1}(\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg(
	\prod_{i=1,2}
	(\beta_{e,t+1})^i((\sigma_e)^i\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg)
		\chi_{e,t+1}(\varsigma_e\,|\,\bm{L}_e)
	\Bigg\}\,,
	\]
has a marginal on $(\smash{\underline{\smash{\sigma}}}_{\delta v},\bm{L}_{\delta v})$ that is fully judicious
(in the sense of Definition~3.45). In the notation of Proposition~7.28, in going between $\hat{q}_{e,t}$ and $\hat{q}_{e,t+3/4}$ we have
	\[
	\textup{\textsf{err}}_v
	= \textup{\textsf{err}}_{v,t}
	= \sum_{e\in\delta v}
	\frac{\delta_{e,t} + \min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}}
		{2^{k(1+\epsilon)}}
	= \frac{\bm{\delta}_t + \bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t}{2^{k(1+\epsilon)}}\,,
	\]
using the notation of (9.89).
It then follows from the bound (7.62) of 
Proposition~7.28 that
	\begin{align}
	\max_{\bm{L}}\Bigg\{
	\bigg|\frac{\psi_{e,t+1}(\bm{L})}{\psi_{e,t+3/4}(\bm{L})}
	-1\bigg|
	+ \max_{\tau\ne\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}}
	\bigg|\frac{(\beta_{e,t+1})^i(\tau\,|\,\bm{L})}
	{(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^i(\tau\,|\,\bm{L})}-1\bigg|
	\Bigg\}
	&\le \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k(1+\epsilon)}}
		\bigg(\delta_{e,t} + 
			\min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}
			+ \textup{\textsf{err}}_{v,t}\bigg)
	\,,\\
	\max_{\bm{L}}\Bigg\{
	\bigg|\frac{(\beta_{e,t+1})^i(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\,|\,\bm{L})}
	{(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^i(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\,|\,\bm{L})}-1\bigg|
	\Bigg\}
	&\le \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}
		\bigg(\delta_{e,t} + 
			\min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}
			+ \textup{\textsf{err}}_{v,t}\bigg)
			\,.
	
	\end{align}
It follows from the bound (7.63) of Proposition~7.28 that
	\begin{align}
	\dddot{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\dot{q}_{e,t},\dot{q}_{e,t+1})
	&\le k^{O(1)}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	1\\1\\1\\ 
	2^{-k\epsilon} \\
	2^{-k\epsilon}
	\end{pmatrix}
		\textup{\textsf{err}}_{v,t}
	+k^{O(1)}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	0&0&0\\
	0&1&1\\
	0&1&1\\
	1&2^{-k}&2^{-k}\\
	1&1&1\\
	\end{pmatrix}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	2^{-k(1+\epsilon)}\delta_{e,t}\\
	2^{-k\epsilon}\delta_{e,t}\\
	2^{-k\epsilon} \min\{ \delta_{e,t}
		+ \ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\} 
	\end{pmatrix} \\
	&\le
	k^{O(1)}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	1\\1\\1\\ 
	2^{-k\epsilon} \\
	2^{-k\epsilon}
	\end{pmatrix} 
	\frac{\bm{\delta}_t+\bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t
		}{2^{k(1+\epsilon)}}
	+k^{O(1)}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	0\\1\\1\\ 0\\1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\frac{\delta_{e,t}
		+\min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}}
		{2^{k\epsilon}}\,.
	
	\end{align}
At time $t+1$ we have
	\[
	\frac{\bm{\zeta}_e(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})}
		{\bm{\zeta}_{e,t+1}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})}
	=
	\frac{\displaystyle
	z_{e,t+1}\sum_{\sigma:\sigma\sim\varsigma}
	\dot{q}_{e,t}(\sigma)
	(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^1(\sigma^1)
	(\beta_{e,t+3/4})^2(\sigma^2)
	 \chi_{e,t+3/4}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})}
	{\displaystyle
	\tilde{z}_{e,t+3/4}
	\sum_{\sigma:\sigma\sim\varsigma}
	\dot{q}_{e,t+1}(\sigma)
	(\beta_{e,t+1})^1(\sigma^1)
	(\beta_{e,t+1})^2(\sigma^2)
	 \chi_{e,t+3/4}(\varsigma\,|\,\bm{L})
	}
	\]
for normalizing constants $\tilde{z}_{e,t+3/4}$ and $z_{e,t+1}$. Combining with (9.91) and (9.92) then gives
	\[
	\delta_{e,t+1}
	+\ddot{\delta}_{e,t+1}
	\le
	\frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}\Bigg(
	\frac{\bm{\delta}_t+\bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t}{2^k}
	+ \delta_{e,t} 
	+ \min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}
	\Bigg)\,.
	\]
This concludes our analysis of the update procedure.\smallskip

\noindent\textbf{\textup{Part~5. Conclusion.}}
Summing the preceding bound over all $e\in\delta v$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	\sum_{t\ge0} (\bm{\delta}_t+\bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t)
	&\le \bm{\delta}_0 + \bm{\ddot{\delta}}_0
	+ 
	\frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}
	\sum_{t\ge0} (\bm{\delta}_t+\bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t)
	\le O(\bm{\delta}_0 + \bm{\ddot{\delta}}_0)
	\le O(k 2^k)\,,\\
	\sum_{t\ge0} 
	(\delta_{e,t} + \min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\})
	&\le 
	\delta_{e,0} + \ddot{\delta}_{e,0}
		+ \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}
		 \sum_{t\ge0}
		\Bigg( \frac{\bm{\delta}_t+\bm{\ddot{\delta}}_t}{2^k}+
		\delta_{e,t} + \min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}
		\Bigg)
	\le O(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
We can use the above bounds with (9.91) to obtain
	\[
	\sum_{t\ge0} \widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{q}_{e,t+3/4},\hat{q}_{e,t+1})
	\le \begin{pmatrix}
	2^{-k} \\ 1 \\ 1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}
	\sum_{t\ge0}
	\bigg(\delta_{e,t} + 
			\min\{\ddot{\delta}_{e,t},1\}
			+ \textup{\textsf{err}}_{v,t}\bigg)
	\le \begin{pmatrix}
	2^{-k} \\ 1 \\ 1
	\end{pmatrix}
	\frac{k^{O(1)} }{2^{k\epsilon}}\,.
	\]	
Combining with (9.90) gives
	\[
	\widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{q}_{e,0},\hat{q}_{e,\infty})
	\le O(1)
	\sum_{t\ge0}\Bigg\{
	\widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{q}_{e,t},\hat{q}_{e,t+3/4})
	+\widehat{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\hat{q}_{e,t+3/4},\hat{q}_{e,t+1})
	\Bigg\}
	\le
	\frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}
	\begin{pmatrix}
	2^{-k}\\
	1\\
	2^k 
	\end{pmatrix}\,.
	\]
(We also see that 
condition~(7.59)
is satisfied by $\hat{q}_{e,t}$ for all $t\ge0$, so that 
the above applications of Proposition~7.28 are justified.)
We also obtain from (9.92) that
	\[
	\dddot{\textup{\textbf{\textsf{ERR}}}}(\dot{q}_{e,0},\dot{q}_{e,\infty})
	\le
	\begin{pmatrix}
	1\\1\\1\\ 
	2^{-k\epsilon} \\ 1
	\end{pmatrix} 
	\frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}\,.
	\]
The above estimates imply that for all $\sigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}^2\setminus\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\}$ we have
	\[\mathbf{P}(\sigma_e=\sigma\,|\,\bm{L}_e=\bm{L})
	\cong \dot{q}_{e,\infty}(\sigma\,|\,\bm{L})
		\hat{q}_{e,\infty}(\sigma\,|\,\bm{L})
	= {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\dot{q}_e(\sigma) {}_\star\hspace{-1pt}\hat{q}_e(\sigma)
		\Bigg( 1 + \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}\Bigg)
	= {}_{*}\omega_e(\sigma)
		\Bigg( 1 + \frac{k^{O(1)}}{2^{k\epsilon}}\Bigg)\,.
	\]
This implies the claimed bounds (9.75).
\end{proof}

Let $\epsilon_2$ be a small absolute constant. Fix $x\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\}$ and $\tau\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize y}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize g}}\}$, and let $v$ be a variable of type $\bm{T}$. Suppose we are given $\omega\in\bm{I}_0$ with marginal $\pi$ such that
	\begin{equation} 
	\sum_{e\in\delta v(x)}\pi_e\Big(
		\sigma^1=\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\,\Big|\,
	\sigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\tau,\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\tau\}\Big)
	\ge k\epsilon_2\,,\end{equation}
where $\pi_e\equiv\pi_{\bm{t}}$ for an edge $e$ of type $\bm{t}$. Let $\Omega$ be the maximizer of (9.41) that is consistent with $\omega$, and let $\bm{\varpi}_{\bm{L},j}$ be the resulting joint distribution of $(\sigma,\upsilon)$. Then there exists a positive absolute constant $\epsilon_3$ (depending only on $\epsilon_2$) such that for every edge $e\in\delta v(x)$ we have
	\[\bm{\varpi}_{\bm{L},j}\Big(
		\upsilon^1=\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize v}}
		\,\Big|\,
		\sigma=\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\tau\Big)
		\ge 1-\frac1{2^{k\epsilon_3}}\]
for $j=j(\bm{t})$ and all clause types $\bm{L}$ such that 
$\bm{L}(j)=\bm{t}$.
The same holds if we exchange the two copies $i=1,2$.

\begin{proof}
The proof is very similar to (but simpler than) that of Lemma~9.8, and we omit the details.
\end{proof}

Consider the setting of Lemma~9.11,
but without assuming a lower bound on $\pi_v(xx)$.
Then
	\[
	\sum_{e\in\delta v} 
	\sum_{\bm{L}\in\mathbb{D}}
	\pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_e)
	\omega_{\bm{L},j(\bm{t}_e)} 
	(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
	\le \frac{k^2}{2^{k\epsilon_4}}

for $\epsilon_4$ as in Lemmas~9.10~and~9.11.

\begin{proof}
In view of Lemma~9.11 it suffices to consider the case $\pi_v(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}) \le 2^{-k/16}$.
Suppose the conclusion of this corollary fails; more explicitly, suppose that
	\[
	\sum_{e\in\delta v} 
	\sum_{\bm{L}\in\mathbb{D}}
	\pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_e)
	\omega_{\bm{L},j(\bm{t}_e)} 
	(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
	\ge \frac{k^4}{2^{k/16}}\,.
	\]
This implies that the assumption
(9.43) of Lemma~9.8 holds, since
	\[
	\sum_{e\in\delta v} 
	\pi_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\,|\, 
	\sigma\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize b}}\}^2)
	\ge \frac{k^4/2^{k/16}}{\pi_v(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}})}
	\ge k^4\,.
	\]
In this case, combining 
Lemma~9.8 and Lemma~9.10 gives that for all $\bm{L},j$ with $\bm{L}(j)=\bm{t}_e$ for $e\in\delta v(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}})$,
	\[
	\omega_{\bm{L},j}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
	\le
	\frac{\omega_{\bm{L},j}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize v}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize v}})}{1-o_k(1)}
	\le
	\frac1{2^{k(1+\epsilon_4)}}\,,
	\]
from which the conclusion of this corollary follows.
\end{proof}

nodes.statement:
On the event that $\mathscr{D}$ expands on type-subsets (Definition~8.2), all non-defective variables are diverse (Definition~9.3); and all strongly 
non-defective clauses are light (Definition~9.4).


\begin{proof} Since we have restricted to $\omega\in\bm{I}_0$ (as has been the case throughout this section), the total number of variables $v$ with frozen spin 
$x_v\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\}$ is close to $n/2$, in any pair frozen configuration that is consistent with $\omega$. Let $S'$ denote the set of all non-diverse variables: then
	\begin{equation}
	|S'|
	= \sum_{v\in V}
	\mathbf{1}\bigg\{
	\pi_v(\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\}) > \frac34 
	\bigg\}
	\le \frac43
	\sum_{v\in V}
	\pi_v(\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\})
	\le \frac{3n}{4}
	\end{equation}
(where the last inequality uses the above observation on the number of variables with $x_v\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}}\}$).

Let $\cancel{\mathbb{D}}\subseteq F$ denote the set of non-diverse clauses; it follows from Definitions~9.3~and~8.2 that $\cancel{\mathbb{D}}\subseteq F_\bullet(S')$. Now let $S\subseteq S'$ denote the subset of non-diverse variables that are non-defective (Definition~3.10), so we see from the above that
$|S| \le |S'| \le 3n/4$. Recall from Remark~6.5
that a clause is termed strongly non-defective if it neighbors only non-defective variables. Let $N\subseteq\cancel{\mathbb{D}}$ denote the set of non-diverse clauses that are strongly non-defective; it follows that $N\subseteq F_\bullet(S)$. Then, on the event that $\mathscr{D}$ expands on type-subsets, it follows from Definition~8.2 that
	\begin{equation}
	|N|
	\le \left\{\hspace{-6pt}\begin{array}{rl}
		n 2^{29k/30} & 
		\text{if }|S|/n \le 4/5\,.\\
		|S| &\text{if } |S|/n \le 1/16\,.
		\end{array}\right.\end{equation}
Next let $\cancel{\mathbb{L}}\subseteq F$ denote the set of all heavy clauses, and let $H\subseteq\cancel{\mathbb{L}}$ denote the subset of heavy clauses that are strongly non-defective. By Proposition~9.16, if $v$ is non-defective but not diverse, then
	\[
	\frac{2^k}{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}}<
	\max\Big\{\cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v),
		\cancel{\mathbb{L}}(v)\Big\}
	\le \cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v)
		+ \cancel{\mathbb{L}}(v)\,,
	\]
where we can take $\epsilon_\infty$ to be much smaller than all the other constants $\epsilon$ in this section. Summing the above over all $v\in S$,
and recalling the definitions
of $\cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v)$ and $\cancel{\mathbb{L}}(v)$
from Definitions~9.3~and~9.4, we obtain
	\begin{equation}
	\frac{2^k |S|}{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}} 
	< \sum_{v\in S}
	\sum_{e\in\delta v}
	\sum_{\bm{L}}
	\pi_{\mathscr{D}}(\bm{L}\,|\,\bm{t}_e)
	\bigg(
	\mathbf{1}\{\bm{L}\in\cancel{\mathbb{D}}
		\cup \cancel{\mathbb{L}}\}\bigg)
	\le \Big(|N| + |H|\Big)k + |S|\,,
	\end{equation}
where the right-hand side of (9.188) is obtained as follows: the contribution from the case of strongly non-defective clause types $\bm{L}$ is bounded by the term $(|N|+|H|)k$, where the factor $k$ accounts for the fact that one clause can neighbor up to $k$ variables. As for the case where $\bm{L}$ fails to be strongly non-defective, we recall from Remark~6.5 that each $v\in S$ neighbors at most one such clause, so the contribution from this case is bounded by the term $|S|$. 

Now note that (9.187) bounds $|N|$ in terms of $|S|$, while (9.188) bounds $|S|$ in terms of $|N|$ and $|H|$. We will close the loop by bounding $|H|$ in terms of $|N|$. In fact we will bound $|E_H|$ where $E_H$ is a subset of edges defined as follows: for any edge $e=(av)$ where $\bm{L}_a=\bm{L}$ and $j=j(\bm{t}_e)$, write $\omega_e\equiv\omega_{\bm{L},j}$. Then let
	\[
	E_H
	\equiv\bigg\{
	e=(av): \textup{$a$ is a strongly non-defective clause
		and }\omega_e(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
		\ge \frac1{2^{k(1+\epsilon_\circ)}}
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Note that a clause belongs to $H$ if and only if it lies incident to $E_H$, so $|H|\le |E_H|$. We will bound
	\[
	|E_H|
	\le \sum_{i=0}^2 |E_H(U_i)|
	\]
where $E_H(U_i)$ denotes the subset of edges in $E_H$ that are incident to $U_i$, and $(U_0,U_1,U_2)$ gives a partition of the set of all non-defective variables: 
	{\setlength{\jot}{0pt}\begin{align*}
	U_0 &\equiv
	\{\text{non-defective variables $v$}:
		\cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v)
		\le 2^{k(1-\epsilon_\infty)},
		\cancel{\mathbb{L}}(v)
		\le 2^{k(1-\epsilon_\infty)}
		\}\,,\\
	U_1 &\equiv
	\{\text{non-defective variables $v$}:
		\cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v)
		\le 2^{k(1-\epsilon_\infty)},
		\cancel{\mathbb{L}}(v)
		> 2^{k(1-\epsilon_\infty)}
		\}\,,\\
	U_2 &\equiv
	\{\text{non-defective variables $v$}:
		\cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v)
		> 2^{k(1-\epsilon_\infty)}	\}\,.
	\end{align*}}
It follows from Proposition~9.16 that
if $v\in U_0$ then $v$ is diverse, and moreover that $\pi_v(x)$ is close to $1/4$ for each $x\in\{\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize -}},\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\}^2$. Thus each $v\in U_0$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma~9.11 --- in particular, Lemma~9.11 has a condition $\pi_v(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}})\ge 2^{-k/16}$ which is certainly guaranteed if $\pi_v(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize +}})$ is close to $1/4$.
It follows by Lemma~9.11 that an edge $e=(av)$ with $v\in U_0$ cannot belong to $E_H$ unless the clause $a$ is non-diverse, which means $a\in N$. Therefore
	\[
	|E_H(U_0)| \le \bigg|\Big\{
		(av) \in E_H : a\in N\Big\}\bigg|
	\le |N|k\,.
	\]
Next, similarly to (9.188) we have the bound
	\begin{equation}
	\frac{2^k |U_1|}{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}}
	<
	\sum_{v\in U_1} \cancel{\mathbb{L}}(v)
	\le |H|k + |U_1| \,.
	\end{equation}
For $v\in U_1$, applying Corollary~9.12 gives
	\begin{equation}
	\sum_{e\in\delta v}
	\sum_{\bm{L}\in\mathbb{D}}
	\pi(\bm{L}|\bm{t}_e)
	\mathbf{1}\Bigg\{ \omega_{\bm{L},j}(\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}}\textup{\texttt{\footnotesize r}})
	\ge \frac1{2^{k(1+\epsilon_\circ)} }\Bigg\}
	\le \frac{{k^2}
		2^{k(1+\epsilon_\circ)}}{2^{k\epsilon_4}}
	\le \frac{2^k}{2^{k\epsilon_\circ}}\,,\end{equation}
where the last bound holds because we took $\epsilon_\circ$ to be much smaller than $\epsilon_4$. Combining with the preceding upper bound on $|U_1|$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	|E_H(U_1)|
	&\le
	\bigg|\Big\{ (av) : a\in N\Big\}\bigg|
	+\bigg|\Big\{ (av)\in E_H : v\in U_1,
		a\in\mathbb{D}\Big\}\bigg|\\
	&\stackrel{(9.190)}{\le}
	|N|k
	+|U_1| \frac{2^k}{2^{k\epsilon_\circ}}
	\stackrel{(9.189)}{\le}
	|N|k
	+|H| \frac{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}}{2^{k\epsilon_\circ}} k
		\bigg(1+o_k(1)\bigg)\,.
	\end{align*}
Finally, similarly to (9.188) and (9.189) we have
	\begin{equation}
	\frac{2^k|U_2| }{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}}
	< \sum_{v\in U_2} \cancel{\mathbb{D}}(v)
	\le |N|k + |U_2|\,,\end{equation}
from which it follows that
	\[
	|E_H(U_2)|
	\le \bigg|\Big\{(av) : v\in U_2\Big\}\bigg|
	\le |U_2| 2^k k^2
	\stackrel{(9.191)}{\le}
	|N| 2^{k\epsilon_\infty}k^3 
	\bigg(1+o_k(1)\bigg)\,.\]
Combining the above bounds gives
	\[|H| \le \sum_{i=0}^2 |E_H(U_i)| 
	\le |N| 2^{k\epsilon_\infty} k^4
		+ |H| \frac{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}}{2^{k\epsilon_\circ}} k^2
	\le
	|N| 2^{k\epsilon_\infty}k^4
	+ \frac{|H|}{2^{k\epsilon_\circ/2}}
	\,,\]
where the last bound holds since we took $\epsilon_\infty$ to be much smaller than $\epsilon_\circ$, as discussed above. Rearranging gives
$|H| \le O(1) |N| 2^{k\epsilon_\infty}k^4$, and combining
with (9.188) gives
	\[
	|S|
	\stackrel{(9.188)}{\le}
	O(1)
	\Big(|N|+|H|\Big) \frac{2^{k\epsilon_\infty}}{2^k} k
	\le \frac{|N| k^{O(1)}}{2^{k(1-2\epsilon_\infty)}}\,.
	\]
Together with the expansion bound 
(9.187)
(which can be applied, since we saw earlier that $|S| \le 3n/4$), we see that the only possibility is for $|S|=|N|=0$. This implies $|H|=0$ and concludes the proof.
\end{proof}
